summary: Habakkuk takes his place like a watchman, waiting for an answer to his complaint. Yahweh tells him to write a vision that may seem delayed but will come, then contrasts the proud with the righteous who live by faith. The rest of the chapter speaks five woes against an arrogant oppressor whose plunder, violence, humiliation, and idols will be answered by reversal and by silence before Yahweh.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the center of Habakkuk’s answer to violence and imperial power: waiting is required, but the oppressor is not finally beyond judgment. It also gives the book’s most remembered line about the righteous living by faith while keeping that line inside a chapter about greed, violence, and delayed justice.

context.author: The headings attribute the book to Habakkuk the prophet, but give no parentage, hometown, or account of the book’s final arrangement.
context.audience: People confronting injustice and imperial violence in a Judean setting, inferred from the book’s complaints rather than from a named dedication.
context.date: The Babylonian crisis provides the setting, around the end of the seventh and beginning of the sixth century BCE; the final composition and arrangement are not dated in the book.
context.setting: Judah under the pressure of Babylonian power, with the Chaldeans named in chapter 1 as the invading force behind the book’s crisis.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic dialogue followed by a taunt: a watchman’s waiting, a written vision, five woes, and a closing call to silence before Yahweh.

outline.heading: Waiting for an answer
outline.note: The speaker stands watch and waits to see what answer will come concerning his complaint.

outline.heading: The written vision and the call to wait
outline.note: Yahweh tells him to write the vision plainly, says it is for an appointed time, and contrasts the puffed-up soul with the righteous who live by faith.

outline.heading: The insatiable oppressor
outline.note: An arrogant figure is pictured as restless and unsatisfied, gathering nations and peoples, but those plundered peoples will turn the taunt back on him.

outline.heading: Gain, security, and witness from the walls
outline.note: The second woe condemns evil gain used to secure a house; even the stone and beam are pictured as witnesses against it.

outline.heading: Blood-built cities and wasted labor
outline.note: The third woe names a town built with blood, while Yahweh’s larger purpose is set against nations wearying themselves for vanity.

outline.heading: Shame returned to the shamer
outline.note: The fourth woe condemns making a neighbor drunk in order to gaze at exposed bodies, and says shame, violence, and destruction will return on the perpetrator.

outline.heading: Mute idols and holy silence
outline.note: The final woe mocks trust in crafted objects that cannot speak or breathe, then closes by setting Yahweh in his holy temple and calling all the earth to silence.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.
keyVerses.why: This verse begins the answer Habakkuk has been waiting for and makes the vision something publicly written and plainly communicated.

keyVerses.text: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it, because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
keyVerses.why: The chapter holds assurance and delay together: the vision is certain, yet the reader is told to wait.

keyVerses.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
keyVerses.why: This sentence gives the chapter’s main contrast between arrogant distortion and righteous life by faith.

keyVerses.text: But Yahweh is in his holy temple. Let all the earth be silent before him!”
keyVerses.why: The closing line answers the noise of taunts, false security, and mute idols with reverent silence before Yahweh.

questions.question: Why does Habakkuk begin this chapter on a watch-post?
questions.answer: Verse 1 continues the complaint from the previous chapter: the speaker is waiting to hear how Yahweh will answer. The images of a watch and ramparts show alert expectation rather than passive resignation. The chapter’s answer begins in verse 2.

questions.question: What is the “vision” that must be written plainly?
questions.answer: The chapter does not give a separate title for the vision, but the answer that follows includes the appointed time, the contrast between pride and faith, and the woes against the oppressor. Writing it on tablets presents it as a message meant to be preserved and read. The wording does not give readers a date to calculate.

questions.question: How can the vision both take time and not delay?
questions.answer: Verse 3 holds two ideas together. From the reader’s perspective, fulfillment may take time and requires waiting; from Yahweh’s answer, the vision is moving toward its appointed end and will not prove false. The verse offers assurance, not a timetable.

questions.question: Who is “his” in “the righteous will live by his faith”?
questions.answer: In WEB, “his faith” most naturally refers to the righteous person. The Hebrew can also be translated “his faithfulness”; interpreters dispute whether the suffix points to the righteous person, God, or the vision. Brenton has “my faith,” reflecting a different Greek reading. These differences affect the emphasis, but the line remains part of the contrast between arrogant power and righteous life while waiting for justice.

questions.question: Who speaks the taunt that begins with “Woe”?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says “all these” will take up a parable and taunting proverb against the arrogant oppressor. In context, these are the nations and peoples he has gathered to himself and plundered. The conquered are imagined as voicing the reversal that the chapter announces.

questions.question: Are the woes only about personal wrongdoing, or about public violence too?
questions.answer: They include both, but the chapter’s scale is public and imperial. The accusations name extortion, evil gain, cutting off many peoples, building a town with blood, violence done to the land, and violence against cities and those who dwell in them. The oppressor’s household, city, and nations are all in view.

questions.question: What does it mean that the stone and beam cry out?
questions.answer: Verse 11 uses poetic speech: the building materials themselves become witnesses against evil gain and shameful security. The point is not that the chapter reports a literal conversation between objects. It says the injustice built into the house cannot finally stay hidden.

questions.question: Why does the chapter condemn giving a neighbor drink?
questions.answer: Verse 15 describes making someone drunk in order to gaze at their naked bodies. Verse 16 answers that coercive exposure with shame returning on the perpetrator. The judgment itself uses harsh bodily humiliation imagery; recognizing the accusation against abuse does not remove that disturbing feature of the poem.

questions.question: Why end with idols and silence before Yahweh?
questions.answer: Verses 18-19 contrast crafted images that cannot teach, speak, or breathe with Yahweh in his holy temple. The final command, “Let all the earth be silent before him,” reverses the false appeal to wood and stone to awaken. The chapter ends by placing all human boasting and idol-making under Yahweh’s presence.

glossary.def: Raised defensive works or walls. In verse 1 the speaker imagines himself stationed there like a watcher waiting for an answer.
The message Yahweh tells Habakkuk to write plainly on tablets. In this chapter it is tied to an appointed time and to the certainty that the answer will come.
The fixed time named in verse 3 for the vision’s fulfillment. The phrase gives assurance that the vision is not false, but it does not give a calendar date.

A cry that introduces accusations in this chapter. It appears in the taunting sayings against the one who gains by extortion, secures a house by evil gain, builds with blood, humiliates a neighbor, and calls on lifeless objects.
The realm of the dead. Verse 5 compares the oppressor’s insatiable appetite for conquest to Sheol and death, which are never satisfied.
The lifeless objects named in verse 18. The next verse stresses the irony: people command wood and stone to awake or arise, but there is no breath within them.
